opus-5.5.text:
I'd push back a little on the framing first. I don't think architecture is *the* bottleneck in some absolute sense; it's more that it's become one of the more interesting places to look again.

For a long time the recipe was clear. You had the transformer, you scaled data and compute, and things got better in a fairly predictable way. Then reinforcement learning on top of that, getting models to reason and think longer, opened up a whole new axis. Those levers are still real and still paying off. But when you squeeze them hard, you start seeing the shape of the container you're working in.

There are a few things I keep running into. One is how these models learn. We train them in big, expensive, offline phases, then freeze them and deploy. A person who's been on a job for six months is much better than they were on day one, because they've been learning continuously from experience. Our models mostly don't do that. You can paper over some of it with context and memory systems, but it's a patch, not a real solution. I suspect fixing that properly needs changes in the underlying machinery, not just better data.

Another is generalization. RL is incredibly powerful within the distribution you train on. But you often see a model get superhuman at a narrow kind of problem, then fall apart on something adjacent that a human would find trivial. Some of that is data and environments, sure. But some of it makes me wonder whether the architecture and training objective are pushing toward brittle, memorized strategies instead of robust understanding.

And there's efficiency. Humans learn from remarkably little data. We're nowhere near that. Throwing more compute at it works, but it's not obviously how you get the next big jump.

So it's less "architecture is broken" and more that the easy wins from the current setup are being harvested, and the next ones may need us to rethink some fundamentals. That's honestly exciting. For a few years it felt like the answer to every question was "scale it." Now there's real research to do again.

r001.rationale: The response says the easy wins from the current setup are being harvested and fundamentals may need rethinking, but it does not specifically call for reconsidering adding parameters to the same MoE and attention operations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on the framing. I don't think architecture is the bottleneck in the way people sometimes mean it, where there's some clever new block waiting to be discovered that unlocks everything. The transformer has been remarkably durable. Most of the "new architecture" papers end up being roughly equivalent to a transformer at scale, or they trade off something you actually cared about.

What I do think is true is that we've gotten most of the easy gains from the recipe we had. Scale up the model, scale up the data, pretrain, do some post-training on top. That worked incredibly well for a while, and it still works, but the returns per unit of effort are clearly flattening in the places that matter. We're running into the limits of how much high-quality human text there is, and we're running into the fact that a model that only predicts the next token isn't naturally set up to do things like think for a long time, check its own work, or learn from its own experience.

So when I say architecture, I mean it more broadly than the neural net diagram. I mean the whole system. How does the model spend compute at test time? How does it decide to spend more on a hard problem and less on an easy one? How does it interact with tools, with an environment, with its own memory? How does the training process actually reward the behaviors we want, rather than just imitating what a person would have written? Reasoning models were an example of this. The underlying network didn't change much. What changed was that we let the model produce a lot of intermediate computation and trained it with reinforcement learning on outcomes. That was an architectural change in the sense I care about, and it produced a step change.

I think the next several step changes look like that. Less about a new attention variant, more about how we structure learning and inference so the model can keep getting better without us hand-feeding it every example. Things like continual learning, better credit assignment over very long horizons, models that can run for hours or days on a task and not lose the thread. Those are genuinely unsolved, and I don't think you solve them by just making the current thing bigger. That's why I'd call it the bottleneck. Compute keeps coming, data is finite, and the question of how you arrange the pieces so that compute turns into capability is the open one.

r001.rationale: The response argues that simply scaling up the current model is yielding flattening returns and says future gains require changing how learning and inference are structured. It also describes the transformer as durable and new attention variants as less central, conveying a call to reconsider scaling the same basic operations.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about calling architecture the bottleneck. There are several things that can limit progress: the training data, the learning objective, the amount of compute, and how effectively the model uses that compute. You can hit a wall with one of those and mistake it for a fundamental limitation of the architecture.

But architecture matters because it determines how a model can learn and reason. If a problem is difficult, can the system spend more time working on it? Can it revise an intermediate conclusion? Can it retain useful information without having to process everything again? Those are important capabilities, and you want the system to learn when and how to use them.

So the question for me is less, “What replaces the transformer?” and more, “What lets us turn additional computation and experience into reliably better answers?” Architecture is part of that, but you have to study it together with the training process.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether architecture alone is the bottleneck and emphasizes using compute and experience effectively, but it does not call for reconsidering parameter scaling within the same MoE and attention operations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much useful computation a model can do when it encounters a new problem. We’ve gotten very good at putting knowledge into models during training. But knowing a lot and being able to work through something you’ve never seen before are different capabilities.

With a standard transformer, you have a fixed amount of computation for each token. Generating a chain of thought gives you a way to spend more computation on a difficult problem, but you’re doing that through a sequence of words. That’s powerful, though I don’t think we should assume it’s the best possible way for a system to think.

So architecture becomes a bottleneck in the sense that it determines how effectively you can use additional compute: can the model maintain a useful internal state, revisit an assumption, or spend more effort on the part of a problem that actually needs it? More data and better training still matter. But I think there’s a lot of room to improve the machinery that turns those resources into reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says architecture affects how effectively models use compute and proposes better internal reasoning machinery, but it does not specifically call for reconsidering scaling parameters within the same MoE and attention operations.
